title: Solve Rational Equations and Inequalities
overview: When is a rational function equal to a value, and when is it bigger or smaller? This section gives you a reliable algebraic routine for rational equations (watch out for **extraneous roots**!) and a sign-table method for rational inequalities – plus technology strategies when algebra gets messy.
objectives: Connect the roots of a rational equation to the zeros of a rational function.
Solve rational equations algebraically and identify extraneous roots.
Solve rational equations graphically or numerically with technology.
Solve rational inequalities with interval tables or the case method, and show solutions on a number line.
Explain the difference between the solution of an equation and of an inequality.
Apply rational equations and inequalities to problems.

lessons.title: Roots of equations and zeros of functions
lessons.body:
Solving the **rational equation** $\dfrac{P(x)}{Q(x)} = 0$ is the same as finding the **zeros** ($x$-intercepts) of the rational function $f(x) = \dfrac{P(x)}{Q(x)}$.

A fraction is zero exactly when its **numerator** is zero and its denominator is **not**. So

$$\frac{x^2 - 9}{x + 1} = 0 \iff x^2 - 9 = 0 \text{ and } x \ne -1 \iff x = \pm 3$$

More generally, to solve $f(x) = g(x)$ you can find where the graphs of $y = f(x)$ and $y = g(x)$ **intersect**, or rearrange to $f(x) - g(x) = 0$ and find the zeros.

lessons.title: Solving rational equations algebraically
lessons.body:
**Strategy**
1. **Factor** every numerator and denominator.
2. State the **restrictions** (values that make any denominator zero).
3. **Multiply both sides by the lowest common denominator** to clear the fractions.
4. Solve the resulting polynomial equation (Chapter 2 techniques).
5. **Reject** any solution that breaks a restriction – these are **extraneous roots** – and check the rest.

**Example:** solve $\dfrac{x + 4}{x - 2} = \dfrac{x - 1}{x - 3}$.

* Restrictions: $x \ne 2$, $x \ne 3$.
* Multiply by $(x - 2)(x - 3)$: $(x + 4)(x - 3) = (x - 1)(x - 2)$.
* Expand: $x^2 + x - 12 = x^2 - 3x + 2$, so $4x = 14$ and $x = 3.5$.
* Check: left $\frac{7.5}{1.5} = 5$, right $\frac{2.5}{0.5} = 5$ ✓.

**Example with an extraneous root:** $\dfrac{2x}{x - 3} = 1 + \dfrac{6}{x - 3}$. Multiply by $(x - 3)$: $2x = x - 3 + 6$, so $x = 3$. But $x \ne 3$! There is **no solution**.

lessons.title: Solving with technology (or a table)
lessons.body:
Some equations, like $\dfrac{x}{x + 2} = \dfrac{x + 3}{3x + 1}$ after clearing fractions, lead to polynomials you cannot factor easily. Then:

* **Graph both sides** and find the intersection points, or
* graph $y = \text{left} - \text{right}$ and find its zeros, or
* use a **table** and narrow down where the sign of left − right changes.

Round answers as asked (often two decimal places) and **remember the restrictions** – a calculator may draw a near-vertical line at an asymptote that is *not* a solution.

**Example:** solve $x - 3 = \dfrac{1}{x}$. Multiply by $x$: $x^2 - 3x - 1 = 0$, $x = \dfrac{3 \pm \sqrt{13}}{2}$, so $x \approx 3.30$ or $x \approx -0.30$. Graphically these are the intersections of the line $y = x - 3$ and the curve $y = \frac{1}{x}$.

```plot
f: x-3 | label=y = x − 3
f: 1/x | label=y = 1/x
domain: -5, 6
range: -6, 5
points: (3.3028,0.3028), (-0.3028,-3.3028)
asymptote x: 0
```

lessons.title: Solving a simple rational inequality
lessons.body:
An **equation** has a few solution **values**; an **inequality** has whole **intervals** of solutions.

**Method 1 – rewrite with 0 on one side (recommended).**

Solve $\dfrac{4}{x - 3} < 1$.
1. Subtract 1: $\dfrac{4}{x - 3} - 1 < 0$.
2. Common denominator: $\dfrac{4 - (x - 3)}{x - 3} < 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{7 - x}{x - 3} < 0$.
3. **Critical values**: zeros of the numerator ($x = 7$) and denominator ($x = 3$).
4. Test each interval:

| Interval | $x < 3$ | $3 < x < 7$ | $x > 7$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| test | 0 | 5 | 8 |
| $\frac{7-x}{x-3}$ | $\frac{+}{-} = -$ | $\frac{+}{+} = +$ | $\frac{-}{+} = -$ |

Solution: $x < 3$ or $x > 7$.

**Method 2 – cases.** You may multiply by $x - 3$ only if you know its sign. **Case 1** $x > 3$: $4 < x - 3 \Rightarrow x > 7$. **Case 2** $x < 3$ (the inequality flips): $4 > x - 3 \Rightarrow x < 7$, combined with $x < 3$ gives $x < 3$. Same answer.

> **Never** multiply both sides by an expression containing $x$ without considering its sign – that is the most common error in this topic.

lessons.title: Interval (sign) tables for harder inequalities
lessons.body:
Solve $\dfrac{x^2 + 5x + 4}{x^2 - 5x + 6} < 0$.

Factor: $\dfrac{(x + 1)(x + 4)}{(x - 2)(x - 3)} < 0$. Critical values in order: $-4, -1, 2, 3$.

| Interval | $x < -4$ | $-4 < x < -1$ | $-1 < x < 2$ | $2 < x < 3$ | $x > 3$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $x + 4$ | − | + | + | + | + |
| $x + 1$ | − | − | + | + | + |
| $x - 2$ | − | − | − | + | + |
| $x - 3$ | − | − | − | − | + |
| quotient | + | − | + | − | + |

Solution: $-4 < x < -1$ or $2 < x < 3$.

**Endpoints:** for $\le$ or $\ge$, include zeros of the **numerator** but **never** include zeros of the denominator (the expression is undefined there).

**Number line:** shade the solution intervals; use open dots at excluded values and closed dots at included ones.

lessons.title: Applications
lessons.body:
**Lens equation.** For a camera with focal length 2.0 cm, the object distance $d$ and image distance $I$ satisfy $d = \dfrac{2.0I}{I - 2.0}$. To focus on an object 10 cm away: $10 = \dfrac{2.0I}{I - 2.0} \Rightarrow 10I - 20 = 2I \Rightarrow I = 2.5$ cm.

**Ratios.** "The ratio of $x + 2$ to $x - 5$ is greater than 3" translates to $\dfrac{x + 2}{x - 5} > 3$, which you solve with an interval table.

**Reading the question carefully:** an *equation* asks "when exactly?", an *inequality* asks "for which values / how long / how many?"

keyTerms.definition: An equation containing at least one rational expression.
A value obtained while solving that does not satisfy the original equation – usually because it is a restriction.
A value of the variable that makes a denominator zero and is therefore excluded.
A zero of the numerator or denominator; the sign of a rational expression can only change at these values.
A table showing the sign of each factor and of the whole expression on each interval between critical values.
An inequality such as $\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} > 0$ whose solution is usually a set of intervals.

formulas.name: Clearing fractions
formulas.meaning: Multiply both sides by the common denominator.

formulas.name: Standard form for inequalities
formulas.meaning: Move everything to one side and combine into a single fraction before testing intervals.

workedExamples.title: Solve using technology
steps: $(x - 3)(x + 1) = 0$, so $x = 3$ or $x = -1$. (A graph of both sides confirms two intersections.)

workedExamples.title: Solve an inequality with a sign table
Ratio problem
workedExamples.problem: The ratio of $x + 2$ to $x - 5$ is greater than 3. Solve for $x$.

misconceptions.myth: To solve $\dfrac{4}{x - 3} < 1$, multiply both sides by $x - 3$ to get $4 < x - 3$.
misconceptions.fact: That is only valid when $x - 3 > 0$. If $x - 3 < 0$ the inequality sign must flip. Use cases, or rewrite with 0 on one side and use a sign table.

misconceptions.myth: Every value I get after clearing fractions is a solution.
misconceptions.fact: Values that make an original denominator zero are **extraneous** and must be rejected.

misconceptions.myth: For $\ge$ inequalities, include all the critical values.
misconceptions.fact: Include zeros of the numerator only; zeros of the denominator are never included.

misconceptions.myth: The solution to an inequality is a list of numbers.
misconceptions.fact: It is usually one or more **intervals**; the boundary values come from the equation.
The denominator is always positive (its discriminant is negative), so the expression is always positive and the inequality has **no solution**.

realWorld.title: Photography
realWorld.body: The lens relation $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{d} + \frac{1}{I}$ rearranges to $d = \frac{fI}{I - f}$, which camera designers solve to place the sensor for sharp focus.

realWorld.title: Work rates
realWorld.body: If one pump fills a tank in 6 h and another in $x$ h, together they take $\frac{6x}{6 + x}$ h. Asking 'how fast must the second pump be to finish in under 4 h?' is a rational inequality.

realWorld.title: Dosage and concentration
realWorld.body: Deciding how long a medication stays above an effective concentration level means solving a rational inequality.

realWorld.title: Budgeting
realWorld.body: Questions like 'how many people must share a bus rental so each pays less than 25 dollars?' lead to inequalities such as $\frac{900}{n} < 25$.

practice.question: Find the $x$-intercepts of $y = \dfrac{x^2 - 16}{x + 1}$.
practice.hint: Set the numerator equal to zero.

practice.question: Explain why $\dfrac{1}{x^2 + 2x + 9} < 0$ has no solution.
practice.solution: $x^2 + 2x + 9 = (x + 1)^2 + 8 > 0$, so the fraction is always positive.

practice.question: Write a rational equation that cannot have $x = 3$ or $x = -5$ as a solution.
practice.solution: For example $\frac{1}{x - 3} + \frac{1}{x + 5} = 1$: both values make a denominator zero.

practice.question: For a camera with focal length 2.0 cm, $d = \dfrac{2.0I}{I - 2.0}$. Find $I$ when $d = 12$ cm.

summary: The roots of $\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} = 0$ are the zeros of $P(x)$ that are not zeros of $Q(x)$ – the $x$-intercepts of the rational function.
To solve algebraically: factor, state restrictions, multiply by the common denominator, solve, and reject extraneous roots.
Equations whose polynomial form is hard to factor can be solved by graphing both sides or using tables.
For inequalities, rewrite with 0 on one side as a single fraction, find the critical values, and test each interval (or use cases).
Never include zeros of the denominator in a solution; include zeros of the numerator only for $\le$ or $\ge$.
An equation's solution is a set of values; an inequality's solution is a set of intervals.

questions.text: Solve $\dfrac{ {{a}} }{x - {{p}}} = {{q}}$ algebraically. State the restriction and check your solution.
questions.modelAnswer:
Restriction: $x \ne {{p}}$.

Multiply both sides by $x - {{p}}$: ${{a}} = {{q}}(x - {{p}})$, so ${{q}}x = {{a + q*p}}$ and $x = \dfrac{ {{a+q*p}} }{ {{q}} } \approx {{p + a/q:4}}$.

Check: $x - {{p}} \approx {{a/q:4}}$ and $\dfrac{ {{a}} }{ {{a/q:4}} } = {{q}}$ ✓. The solution is not the restriction, so it is valid.

questions.text: Solve $\dfrac{x + {{a}}}{x - {{b}}} = \dfrac{x - {{c}}}{x - {{b+1}}}$. State the restrictions and check your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
Restrictions: $x \ne {{b}}$, $x \ne {{b+1}}$.

Cross-multiply: $(x + {{a}})(x - {{b+1}}) = (x - {{c}})(x - {{b}})$.

Expand: $x^2 + {{a-b-1}}x - {{a*(b+1)}} = x^2 - {{b+c}}x + {{b*c}}$.

The $x^2$ terms cancel: $({{a-b-1}} + {{b+c}})x = {{b*c}} + {{a*(b+1)}}$, so ${{a+c-1}}x = {{b*c+a*(b+1)}}$ and

$x = \dfrac{ {{b*c+a*(b+1)}} }{ {{a+c-1}} } \approx {{(b*c+a*(b+1))/(a+c-1):4}}$.

This is not a restriction. Check: substitute into both sides; both equal approximately {{((b*c+a*(b+1))/(a+c-1)+a)/((b*c+a*(b+1))/(a+c-1)-b):4}}.

rubric.point: Expands and simplifies to a linear equation

questions.text: Solve $x + \dfrac{ {{r1*r2}} }{x} = {{r1+r2}}$ algebraically and verify your solutions. Explain how the solutions relate to the graphs of $y = x + \dfrac{ {{r1*r2}} }{x}$ and $y = {{r1+r2}}$.
questions.modelAnswer:
Restriction $x \ne 0$. Multiply by $x$: $x^2 + {{r1*r2}} = {{r1+r2}}x$, so $x^2 - {{r1+r2}}x + {{r1*r2}} = 0$.

Factor: $(x - {{r1}})(x - {{r2}}) = 0$, so $x = {{r1}}$ or $x = {{r2}}$.

Verify: ${{r1}} + \frac{ {{r1*r2}} }{ {{r1}} } = {{r1}} + {{r2}} = {{r1+r2}}$ ✓; ${{r2}} + \frac{ {{r1*r2}} }{ {{r2}} } = {{r1+r2}}$ ✓.

The solutions are the $x$-coordinates of the points where the curve $y = x + \frac{ {{r1*r2}} }{x}$ meets the horizontal line $y = {{r1+r2}}$.

questions.text: A student solves $\dfrac{2x}{x - {{h}}} = 1 + \dfrac{ {{2*h}} }{x - {{h}}}$ and gets $x = {{h}}$. Is the student correct? Explain fully.
questions.modelAnswer:
Multiply both sides by $x - {{h}}$: $2x = (x - {{h}}) + {{2*h}}$, so $2x = x + {{h}}$ and $x = {{h}}$.

But $x = {{h}}$ makes both denominators zero, so it is a **restriction**: the original equation is undefined there. $x = {{h}}$ is an **extraneous root**, and the equation has **no solution**.

The student did the algebra correctly but forgot to check the answer against the restrictions. Graphically, the left side equals $2 + \frac{ {{2*h}} }{x - {{h}}}$ and the right side equals $1 + \frac{ {{2*h}} }{x - {{h}}}$; they always differ by 1, so the graphs never meet.

rubric.point: Identifies x = h as a restriction

questions.text: Solve $\dfrac{ {{a}} }{x - {{p}}} < {{q}}$ without technology. Show your work with an interval table and illustrate the solution on a number line (describe it in words).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the critical value that comes from the numerator.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the full solution and describe the number line.

questions.modelAnswer:
$\dfrac{ {{a}} }{x - {{p}}} - {{q}} < 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{ {{a}} - {{q}}(x - {{p}})}{x - {{p}}} < 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{ {{a+q*p}} - {{q}}x}{x - {{p}}} < 0$.

Critical values: $x = {{p}}$ (denominator) and $x = \frac{ {{a+q*p}} }{ {{q}} } \approx {{p+a/q:3}}$ (numerator).

| Interval | $x < {{p}}$ | ${{p}} < x < {{p+a/q:3}}$ | $x > {{p+a/q:3}}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| numerator | + | + | − |
| denominator | − | + | + |
| quotient | − | + | − |

Solution: $x < {{p}}$ or $x > {{p+a/q:3}}$. Number line: open dots at {{p}} and {{p+a/q:3}}, shading to the left of {{p}} and to the right of {{p+a/q:3}}.

rubric.point: Rewrites as a single fraction compared with 0

questions.text: Solve $\dfrac{x^2 + 5x + 4}{x^2 - 5x + 6} < 0$ algebraically using an interval table.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the critical value from the numerator.

questions.text: Explain the difference between the solution to the equation $\dfrac{4}{x - 3} = 1$ and the solution to the inequality $\dfrac{4}{x - 3} > 1$. Use a graph or number line description in your explanation.
questions.modelAnswer:
The **equation** has a single solution: $4 = x - 3$, so $x = 7$ – the one $x$-value where the graph of $y = \frac{4}{x - 3}$ meets the line $y = 1$.

The **inequality** asks where the curve is **above** the line. This happens for all $x$ between the vertical asymptote and the intersection: $3 < x < 7$ – an interval with infinitely many values. The equation's solution ($x = 7$) is a boundary of the inequality's solution, and the restriction $x = 3$ is the other boundary (excluded).

rubric.point: Links the boundary to the equation and the restriction

questions.modelAnswer:
The numerator 1 is positive, so the sign of the expression is the sign of the denominator.

The discriminant of $x^2 + {{b}}x + {{c}}$ is ${{b}}^2 - 4({{c}}) = {{b*b-4*c}} < 0$, so the quadratic has no real zeros. Since it opens upward and never crosses the $x$-axis, it is **always positive**. (Completing the square: $\left(x + \frac{ {{b}} }{2}\right)^2 + {{c-b*b/4:3}} > 0$.)

Therefore the fraction is always positive and can never be less than 0: no solution.

rubric.point: Shows the quadratic is always positive (discriminant or completing the square)

questions.text: The ratio of $x + {{a}}$ to $x - {{b}}$ is greater than {{k}}. Solve for $x$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Upper bound of the solution interval.

questions.modelAnswer:
$\dfrac{x + {{a}}}{x - {{b}}} > {{k}} \Rightarrow \dfrac{x + {{a}} - {{k}}(x - {{b}})}{x - {{b}}} > 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{ {{a+k*b}} - {{k-1}}x}{x - {{b}}} > 0$.

Critical values: $x = {{b}}$ and $x = \dfrac{ {{a+k*b}} }{ {{k-1}} } \approx {{(a+k*b)/(k-1):4}}$.

Test: left of {{b}} the numerator is positive and the denominator negative → negative. Between → both positive → positive. Right of {{(a+k*b)/(k-1):4}} → numerator negative → negative.

Solution: ${{b}} < x < {{(a+k*b)/(k-1):4}}$.

questions.text: Solve $x - {{k}} = \dfrac{1}{x}$ algebraically and explain how you could verify the solutions graphically. Give answers to two decimal places.
questions.modelAnswer:
Restriction $x \ne 0$. Multiply by $x$: $x^2 - {{k}}x = 1$, so $x^2 - {{k}}x - 1 = 0$.

$x = \dfrac{ {{k}} \pm \sqrt{ {{k*k}} + 4} }{2}$, giving $x \approx {{(k+sqrt(k*k+4))/2:3}}$ or $x \approx {{(k-sqrt(k*k+4))/2:3}}$.

Neither is 0, so both are valid. Graphically: plot $y = x - {{k}}$ and $y = \frac{1}{x}$; they intersect at two points whose $x$-coordinates are these solutions (one on each branch of the hyperbola).

questions.text: For a camera lens with focal length 2.0 cm, the object distance $d$ and the image distance $I$ (both in cm) are related by $d = \dfrac{2.0I}{I - 2.0}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find $I$ when the object is {{d}} cm away.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Interpret the asymptotes of the relation in context.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) ${{d}} = \dfrac{2.0I}{I - 2.0}$: ${{d}}I - {{2*d}} = 2.0I$, so ${{d-2}}I = {{2*d}}$ and $I = \dfrac{ {{2*d}} }{ {{d-2}} } \approx {{2*d/(d-2):3}}$ cm.

(b) The vertical asymptote $I = 2.0$: as the image distance approaches the focal length, the object distance grows without bound – objects very far away focus at the focal length. The horizontal asymptote $d = 2.0$: a very large image distance corresponds to an object just beyond the focal length. Only $I > 2.0$ (and $d > 2.0$) are physically meaningful.

questions.text: Write a rational equation that cannot have $x = {{p}}$ or $x = -{{q}}$ as a solution, and that does have at least one solution. Solve your equation and explain why it meets the conditions.
questions.modelAnswer:
Make ${{p}}$ and $-{{q}}$ restrictions by putting $x - {{p}}$ and $x + {{q}}$ in denominators. Example:

$$\frac{1}{x - {{p}}} + \frac{1}{x + {{q}}} = 0$$

Multiply by $(x - {{p}})(x + {{q}})$: $(x + {{q}}) + (x - {{p}}) = 0$, so $2x = {{p-q}}$ and $x = {{(p-q)/2:3}}$.

Check: $x = {{(p-q)/2:3}}$ is neither {{p}} nor $-{{q}}$, so it is a valid solution. The values {{p}} and $-{{q}}$ make a denominator zero, so they can never be solutions of this equation.

rubric.point: Equation with both values as restrictions
Equation has at least one solution
Explains why the conditions are met

questions.text: Solve $\dfrac{ {{a}} }{x - {{p}}} > 1$ using the **case method** (consider the sign of $x - {{p}}$). Then confirm your answer with a test point in each interval.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show both cases and the check.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Case 1:** $x - {{p}} > 0$ ($x > {{p}}$). Multiply without flipping: ${{a}} > x - {{p}}$, so $x < {{a+p}}$. Combined: ${{p}} < x < {{a+p}}$.

**Case 2:** $x - {{p}} < 0$ ($x < {{p}}$). Multiply and flip: ${{a}} < x - {{p}}$, so $x > {{a+p}}$. This contradicts $x < {{p}}$: no solutions.

Solution: ${{p}} < x < {{a+p}}$.

Test points: $x = {{p-1}}$: $\frac{ {{a}} }{-1} = -{{a}} > 1$? No. $x = {{p}}.5$: $\frac{ {{a}} }{0.5} = {{2*a}} > 1$ ✓. $x = {{a+p+1}}$: $\frac{ {{a}} }{ {{a+1}} } < 1$ ✗. Confirmed.

rubric.point: Case 2 correct with flipped inequality and contradiction

questions.text: Solve $\dfrac{3}{x + 2} \le \dfrac{4}{x + 3}$. Illustrate the solution on a number line (describe which dots are open and closed).
questions.modelAnswer:
$\dfrac{3}{x + 2} - \dfrac{4}{x + 3} \le 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{3(x + 3) - 4(x + 2)}{(x + 2)(x + 3)} \le 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{1 - x}{(x + 2)(x + 3)} \le 0$.

Critical values: $-3, -2, 1$.

| Interval | $x < -3$ | $-3 < x < -2$ | $-2 < x < 1$ | $x > 1$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $1 - x$ | + | + | + | − |
| $(x+2)(x+3)$ | + | − | + | + |
| quotient | + | − | + | − |

At $x = 1$ the expression equals 0, so it is included. Solution: $-3 < x < -2$ or $x \ge 1$. Number line: open dots at −3 and −2 (restrictions), closed dot at 1.

$\dfrac{x}{x+1} - \dfrac{2x}{x-2} \ge 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{x(x - 2) - 2x(x + 1)}{(x + 1)(x - 2)} \ge 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{-x^2 - 4x}{(x + 1)(x - 2)} \ge 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{-x(x + 4)}{(x + 1)(x - 2)} \ge 0$.

Critical values $-4, -1, 0, 2$. Test points: $x = -5$: $\frac{-5}{28} < 0$; $x = -2$: $\frac{4}{4} > 0$; $x = -0.5$: negative; $x = 1$: $\frac{-5}{-2} > 0$; $x = 3$: negative.

Include zeros of the numerator ($-4$ and $0$), exclude restrictions ($-1$, $2$).

Solution: $-4 \le x < -1$ or $0 \le x < 2$.

rubric.point: Sign analysis on all five intervals

questions.text: Determine the $x$-intercepts of $y = \dfrac{x^2 - {{n*n}}}{x + {{m}}}$. Explain the connection between the roots of a rational equation and the zeros of the corresponding rational function.
questions.modelAnswer:
Set the numerator equal to zero: $x^2 - {{n*n}} = 0 \Rightarrow x = \pm{{n}}$. Neither makes the denominator $x + {{m}}$ zero, so the $x$-intercepts are $({{n}}, 0)$ and $(-{{n}}, 0)$.

The roots of the equation $\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} = 0$ are exactly the zeros of the function $f(x) = \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}$: the zeros of the numerator that are not restrictions.

questions.text: Decompose $\dfrac{ {{A+B}}x + {{3*B-A}} }{x^2 + 2x - 3}$ into partial fractions of the form $\dfrac{A}{x + 3} + \dfrac{B}{x - 1}$. Check by recombining.
